The first ten lectures built one argument. A black hole is what you get when
gravity wins completely (lectures 1 and 2); understanding it needs special
relativity (lecture 3) and then general relativity (lectures 4 and 5); what we
actually see of one is light, shifted and beamed (lecture 6); and the light
comes from matter falling in, which sets how bright a black hole can be and how
fast it can grow (lectures 7 to 9). Lecture 10 added a second messenger that is
not light at all. **This page collects the ideas in one place and gives you
problems that pull them together.**

## The ideas, lecture by lecture

- **Lecture 1.** [Escape velocity](../scales-and-schwarzschild/index.qmd#escape-velocity)
  and [the Schwarzschild radius](../scales-and-schwarzschild/index.qmd#the-schwarzschild-radius),
  $r_S = 2GM/c^2$.
- **Lecture 2.** [The no-hair theorem](../spinning-bhs-and-tidal/index.qmd#the-no-hair-theorem);
  [spinning black holes](../spinning-bhs-and-tidal/index.qmd#spinning-black-holes) —
  the horizon, the ergosphere and the ISCO, and how each depends on $a_*$;
  [tidal forces](../spinning-bhs-and-tidal/index.qmd#tidal-forces),
  $F_t = 2GMms/d^3$.
- **Lecture 3.** [Time dilation](../special-relativity/index.qmd#time-dilation),
  [length contraction](../special-relativity/index.qmd#length-contraction) and
  why it happens [only along the direction of motion](../special-relativity/index.qmd#why-length-contraction-only-happens-along-the-direction-of-motion),
  and the [relativistic Doppler shift](../special-relativity/index.qmd#relativistic-doppler-shift-of-light).
- **Lecture 4.** Gravity as geometry, and [the classic tests](../general-relativity/index.qmd#the-classic-tests)
  of general relativity.
- **Lecture 5.** [Gravitational redshift](../strong-gravity/index.qmd#gravitational-redshift),
  [gravitational time dilation](../strong-gravity/index.qmd#gravitational-time-dilation),
  and a first look at [gravitational waves](../strong-gravity/index.qmd#gravitational-waves).
- **Lecture 6.** [Light as a wave](../seeing-black-holes/index.qmd#light-is-a-wave)
  ($c = \lambda\nu$, $E = h\nu$), [the Doppler shift](../seeing-black-holes/index.qmd#the-doppler-shift-recalled)
  and [Doppler beaming](../seeing-black-holes/index.qmd#doppler-beaming).
- **Lecture 7.** [Where falling stops paying: the ISCO](../accretion-efficiency/index.qmd#where-falling-stops-paying-the-isco),
  [the luminosity of accretion](../accretion-efficiency/index.qmd#the-luminosity-of-accretion),
  $L = \eta\dot M c^2$, and [blackbody radiation](../accretion-efficiency/index.qmd#blackbody-radiation-and-effective-temperature).
- **Lecture 8.** [The Eddington limit](../eddington-limit/index.qmd#the-eddington-limit),
  [the Eddington accretion rate](../eddington-limit/index.qmd#the-eddington-accretion-rate),
  and [what accreting matter looks like](../eddington-limit/index.qmd#what-accreting-matter-looks-like).
- **Lecture 9.** [Growing at the Eddington limit](../black-hole-growth/index.qmd#growing-at-the-eddington-limit)
  and [why efficiency slows growth](../black-hole-growth/index.qmd#why-efficiency-slows-growth).
- **Lecture 10.** [How big the effect of a gravitational wave is](../gravitational-waves/index.qmd#how-big-is-the-effect),
  and [the first, indirect evidence](../gravitational-waves/index.qmd#the-first-evidence-was-indirect).

## Multiple choice

**Problem 1.** According to the no-hair theorem, which quantities completely
describe a black hole once it has settled down?

a. Its mass alone
b. Its mass and its spin
c. Its mass, its spin and its electric charge
d. Its mass, its spin, its electric charge and what it formed from

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(c).** Mass, spin (angular momentum) and charge are the only three numbers a
settled black hole keeps. Everything else about what fell in — whether it was
hydrogen or iron, a star or a cloud of gas — is the "hair" the theorem says a
black hole does not have. That is exactly why (d) is wrong.
::::

**Problem 2.** Radio waves and X-rays both travel at the speed of light.
Compared with a radio photon, an X-ray photon has

a. a longer wavelength and a higher energy
b. a shorter wavelength and a lower frequency
c. a shorter wavelength, a higher frequency and a higher energy
d. the same energy, because both travel at $c$

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(c).** Wavelength, frequency and photon energy are locked together:
$c = \lambda\nu$ says a shorter wavelength means a higher frequency, and
$E = h\nu$ says a higher frequency means a higher energy. Traveling at $c$ says
nothing about the energy, which rules out (d).
::::

**Problem 3.** A probe falls toward a black hole, sending out a radio pulse
once every second by its own clock. As the probe nears the horizon, a distant
observer receives the pulses

a. closer together, and shifted to shorter wavelengths
b. closer together, and shifted to longer wavelengths
c. farther apart, and shifted to shorter wavelengths
d. farther apart, and shifted to longer wavelengths

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(d).** Deep in the black hole's gravity the probe's clock runs slow as seen
from far away, so its once-a-second pulses arrive farther and farther apart.
The radio waves themselves are clocks too, so the same effect stretches their
wavelength: gravitational redshift. (The probe is also moving away from the
observer, and its Doppler shift works in the same direction.)
::::

**Problem 4.** A gravitational-wave detector can just measure a strain of
$10^{-22}$. A particular kind of merger produces a strain of $10^{-21}$ at Earth
when it happens $100\ \mathrm{Mpc}$ away. Out to what distance could the
detector see an identical merger?

a. $100\ \mathrm{Mpc}$
b. $316\ \mathrm{Mpc}$
c. $1000\ \mathrm{Mpc}$
d. $10\,000\ \mathrm{Mpc}$

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(c).** Strain falls off as $1/d$, so to shrink it by a factor of 10 the
merger has to be 10 times farther away. Answer (b) is what you get from
$1/d^2$, which is how *flux* falls off, not strain.
::::

**Problem 5.** Which of these statements about the ergosphere is true?

a. It lies inside the event horizon.
b. It exists only around a spinning black hole.
c. It is a perfect sphere.
d. Inside it, light aimed against the black hole's spin travels against the
   spin.

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(b).** The ergosphere is where frame dragging forces everything, even light,
to move with the spin — so it needs a spin, and (d) is exactly backward. It
lies *outside* the horizon, touching it only at the poles, which rules out (a),
and it is flattened rather than spherical, which rules out (c).
::::

**Problem 6.** Steve flies past Alex at $0.8c$, holding a meter stick
*perpendicular* to his direction of motion. Which of these do Steve and Alex
agree on?

a. The length of the meter stick
b. The time between two ticks of Steve's watch
c. The length of Steve's spaceship
d. None of the above

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(a).** Length contraction happens only along the direction of motion, and the
stick is held across it, so both measure one meter. The ship lies along the
motion, so Alex measures it contracted (c); and Alex measures Steve's watch
running slow (b).
::::

**Problem 7.** A person stands near one of four black holes. Where is the
tidal stretching across the person largest?

a. $1000\ \mathrm{km}$ from a $10\,M_\odot$ black hole
b. $2000\ \mathrm{km}$ from a $10\,M_\odot$ black hole
c. $1000\ \mathrm{km}$ from a $20\,M_\odot$ black hole
d. $2000\ \mathrm{km}$ from a $20\,M_\odot$ black hole

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(c).** The tidal force goes as $M/d^3$ for a person of fixed size. Doubling
the mass doubles it; doubling the distance cuts it by a factor of 8. So the
larger mass at the smaller distance wins, and (b) is the weakest of the four.
::::

**Problem 8.** Two astronauts fall feet first through the event horizons of two
black holes, one of $10\,M_\odot$ and one of $10^6\,M_\odot$. Compared with the
tidal stretching at the smaller black hole's horizon, the stretching at the
larger one's horizon is

a. $10^{10}$ times smaller
b. $10^{5}$ times smaller
c. the same
d. $10^{10}$ times larger

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(a).** At the horizon $d = r_S \propto M$, so the tidal force goes as
$M/r_S^3 \propto M/M^3 = 1/M^2$. The larger black hole is $10^5$ times more
massive, so the stretching is $(10^5)^2 = 10^{10}$ times *gentler*. Bigger
black hole, gentler crossing.
::::

## Short answer

**Problem 9.** Two black holes have the same mass and both accrete at their
Eddington limits. One is not spinning ($\eta = 5.7\%$); the other spins as fast
as possible, with its gas orbiting in the same direction as the spin
($\eta = 42\%$). Which one grows faster, and why? Roughly how many times
faster?

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**The non-spinning one.** Both are held to the same luminosity, the Eddington
luminosity, which depends only on the mass. The efficient black hole makes that
luminosity out of less gas, so it is allowed to accrete less; and of the gas it
does accrete, it sends a larger fraction away as light instead of keeping it as
mass. Both effects are in the Salpeter time,
$t_S \propto \eta/(1-\eta)$:

$$
\frac{t_S(42\%)}{t_S(5.7\%)} = \frac{0.42/0.58}{0.057/0.943} \approx 12 .
$$

The non-spinning black hole's Salpeter time is about 12 times shorter, so it grows about 12 times faster.
::::

**Problem 10.** The spectral lines of a white dwarf are found at slightly longer
wavelengths than the same lines measured in a laboratory, even after the star's
motion toward or away from us has been corrected for. Explain how this tests
general relativity, and why the effect is much larger for a white dwarf than
for the Sun.

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
General relativity predicts **gravitational redshift**: light climbing out of a
gravitational well arrives at longer wavelength, equivalently, clocks deep in
the well — including the atoms emitting the lines — run slow as seen from far
away. The size of the shift is set by $r_S/R$, how compact the star is. A white
dwarf has about the Sun's mass packed into a radius about a hundred times
smaller, so $r_S/R$, and with it the redshift, is about a hundred times larger.
::::

**Problem 11.** The Eddington luminosity,
$L_{\mathrm{Edd}} = 4\pi c G M m_p/\sigma_T$, contains the *proton's* mass but
the *electron's* cross section. Explain why.

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Eddington luminosity is where the outward push of light on the gas balances
the inward pull of gravity. Gravity pulls on the gas through its mass, and
nearly all the mass of an electron–proton pair is the proton's. Light pushes on
the gas through scattering, and the electron scatters light far more
effectively than the proton, so its Thomson cross section sets the push. The
electrical attraction between them keeps each electron and proton together, so
the push on one and the pull on the other act on the same pair.
::::

## Calculations

**Problem 12.** Alex's spaceship shines a laser whose light is $600\ \mathrm{nm}$
in the ship's own frame. Steve, watching from far away, measures it at
$300\ \mathrm{nm}$. Is the ship approaching Steve or receding from him, and how
fast is it going?

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The light arrives at a *shorter* wavelength, blueshifted, so **the ship is
approaching.** For an approaching source the relativistic Doppler shift is

$$
\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{emit}}}
  = \left(\frac{1 - \beta}{1 + \beta}\right)^{1/2} .
$$

*Do the units make sense?* Both sides are ratios of pure numbers, so the units
pass straight through. Setting the ratio to $300/600 = 1/2$ and squaring,

$$
\frac{1 - \beta}{1 + \beta} = \frac{1}{4}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad 4 - 4\beta = 1 + \beta
\quad\Rightarrow\quad \beta = 0.6 .
$$

The ship approaches at $0.6c$.
::::

**Problem 13.** A neutron star has a mass of $2.0\,M_\odot$ and a radius of
$12\ \mathrm{km}$.

a. Light leaves its surface with a wavelength of $400\ \mathrm{nm}$. At what
   wavelength does a distant observer see it?
b. How small would a star of any mass have to be, as a multiple of its own
   Schwarzschild radius, for light from its surface to arrive at *twice* its
   emitted wavelength?

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
**(a)** First the Schwarzschild radius, substituting with the units attached
and writing the mass conversion as a fraction:

$$
M = 2.0\,M_\odot \times \frac{1.9891 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}{1\,M_\odot}
  = 3.978 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_S &= \frac{2GM}{c^2} \\[0.8em]
  &= \frac{2\left(6.6732 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\right)
          \left(3.978 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}\right)}
         {\left(2.998 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)^2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The units are $\mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} \times \mathrm{g} \div
\mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-2}} = \mathrm{cm}$. *Do the units make sense?* A radius is a
length, so yes. Then $r_S = 5.91 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm} = 5.91\
\mathrm{km}$, and with $R = 12\ \mathrm{km}$, $r_S/R = 0.492$. The observed
wavelength is

$$
\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}} = \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{emit}}}{\sqrt{1 - r_S/R}}
  = \frac{400\ \mathrm{nm}}{\sqrt{1 - 0.492}} = 561\ \mathrm{nm} .
$$

**(b)** Twice the wavelength means $\sqrt{1 - r_S/R} = 1/2$, so
$1 - r_S/R = 1/4$ and $R = \tfrac{4}{3}\,r_S$. The star would have to be only a
third larger than its own Schwarzschild radius — far more compact than any
neutron star.
::::

**Problem 14.** Alex's spaceship is $50\ \mathrm{m}$ long when measured at rest.
As it flies past, Steve measures it to be $40\ \mathrm{m}$ long. How fast is it
moving relative to Steve?

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The rest length is the proper length, and a moving ship is contracted:
$L = L_0/\gamma$. So $\gamma = 50\ \mathrm{m}/40\ \mathrm{m} = 1.25$; the
meters cancel, and a Lorentz factor is a pure number, so the units make sense.
Then

$$
\beta = \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{\gamma^2}} = \sqrt{1 - 0.64} = 0.6 ,
$$

and the ship moves at $0.6c$.
::::

## Putting it all together

These two problems need several lectures at once, like the exam's 20-point
calculation. Getting the concepts to fit together matters more than the final
number.

**Problem 15.**

:::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: how hot is gas falling into a stellar-mass black hole?"}
**The question.** A non-spinning black hole of $10\,M_\odot$ is accreting at
its Eddington limit. (a) At what rate is it accreting mass, in solar masses per
year? (b) Estimate the temperature of the glowing gas by assuming that its
whole luminosity is radiated as a blackbody from a sphere the size of its ISCO.
(c) At what wavelength does that blackbody peak, and what kind of light is
that?

**What the problem needs, and where it comes from.** A non-spinning black hole
has radiative efficiency $\eta = 5.7\%$ and $r_{\mathrm{ISCO}} = 3r_S$
([lecture 7](../accretion-efficiency/index.qmd#where-falling-stops-paying-the-isco)).
"At its Eddington limit" means $L = L_{\mathrm{Edd}}$
([lecture 8](../eddington-limit/index.qmd#the-eddington-limit)). Accretion
turns mass into light by $L = \eta\dot M c^2$, and a blackbody sphere obeys
$L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$ ([lecture 7](../accretion-efficiency/index.qmd#blackbody-radiation-and-effective-temperature)).

**The luminosity.** With
$M = 10\,M_\odot \times (1.9891 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}/1\,M_\odot)
= 1.989 \times 10^{34}\ \mathrm{g}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
L_{\mathrm{Edd}} = {} & \frac{4\pi c G M m_p}{\sigma_T} \\[0.8em]
  = {} & 4\pi \left(2.998 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right) \\[0.8em]
  & \times \left(6.6732 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}\right)
          \left(1.989 \times 10^{34}\ \mathrm{g}\right) \\[0.8em]
  & \times \frac{1.6726 \times 10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g}}
         {6.6524 \times 10^{-25}\ \mathrm{cm^2}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Across all four lines, the top carries $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} \times \mathrm{cm^3\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}
\times \mathrm{g} \times \mathrm{g} = \mathrm{g\,cm^4\,s^{-3}}$, and dividing
by $\mathrm{cm^2}$ leaves $\mathrm{g\,cm^2\,s^{-3}}$. *Do the units make
sense?* That is an erg per second, a luminosity, so yes.

$$
L_{\mathrm{Edd}} = 1.26 \times 10^{39}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}
$$

**(a) The accretion rate.** Solving $L = \eta\dot M c^2$ for $\dot M$,

$$
\dot M = \frac{L}{\eta c^2}
  = \frac{1.26 \times 10^{39}\ \mathrm{g\,cm^2\,s^{-3}}}
         {0.057\left(2.998 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)^2} .
$$

The $\mathrm{cm^2}$ cancel and two of the three inverse seconds cancel, leaving
$\mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}$ — a mass per unit time, which is what an accretion rate
is. So $\dot M = 2.45 \times 10^{19}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}$, and converting,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 2.45 \times 10^{19}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}
  \times \frac{3.156 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}}{1\ \mathrm{yr}} \\[0.8em]
& \times \frac{1\,M_\odot}{1.9891 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{g}}
  = 3.9 \times 10^{-7}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

**(b) The temperature.** The Schwarzschild radius is
$r_S = 2GM/c^2 = 2.95 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm}$, about $30\ \mathrm{km}$, so
the sphere has $R = 3r_S = 8.86 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm}$. Solving the
blackbody luminosity gives $T = \left(L/4\pi R^2 \sigma\right)^{1/4}$.
The denominator first:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4\pi R^2 \sigma = {} & 4\pi \left(8.86 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{cm}\right)^2 \\[0.8em]
  & \times \left(5.6696 \times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{erg\,cm^{-2}\,K^{-4}\,s^{-1}}\right) \\[0.8em]
  = {} & 5.59 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,K^{-4}} ,
\end{aligned}
$$

where the square centimeters cancel. Then

$$
T = \left(\frac{1.26 \times 10^{39}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}}
     {5.59 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,K^{-4}}}\right)^{1/4} .
$$

The ergs and the seconds cancel, leaving $\mathrm{K^4}$, and the fourth root is
kelvin. *Do the units make sense?* A temperature, so yes. Then
$T = 1.2 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{K}$.

**(c) The peak.** From Wien's law,
$\lambda_{\max} = (0.290\ \mathrm{cm\,K})/(1.2 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{K})
= 2.4 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.24\ \mathrm{nm}$. **X-rays** — which is
why accreting stellar-mass black holes are found with X-ray telescopes.

Notice what the efficiency did: it set the accretion rate in (a) and dropped out
of (b) entirely. The temperature depends only on the luminosity and the size.
::::

**Problem 16.** A $10^6\,M_\odot$ black hole spins as fast as possible, but the
gas around it orbits *against* the spin, so its ISCO is at $4.5r_S$ and its
radiative efficiency is $3.8\%$. It shines at 10% of its Eddington luminosity.

a. At what rate is it accreting mass, in solar masses per year?
b. Using the same blackbody-sphere estimate as problem 15, how hot is the gas,
   and where does its light peak?
c. Compare your temperature with problem 15's. Why is gas around the heavier
   black hole *cooler*?

:::: {.callout-tip .help-solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The units work exactly as in problem 15, so only the numbers are shown here.

With $M = 1.989 \times 10^{39}\ \mathrm{g}$, the Eddington luminosity is
$1.26 \times 10^{44}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ — $10^5$ times problem 15's,
because it is proportional to the mass — and 10% of it is
$L = 1.26 \times 10^{43}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$.

**(a)** The accretion rate is $\dot M = L/\eta c^2 = 3.68 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}
= 5.8 \times 10^{-3}\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr^{-1}}$.

**(b)** The Schwarzschild radius is $r_S = 2.95 \times 10^{11}\ \mathrm{cm}$, so
$R = 4.5r_S = 1.33 \times 10^{12}\ \mathrm{cm}$, and
$T = (L/4\pi R^2\sigma)^{1/4} = 3.2 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{K}$. The peak is at
$\lambda_{\max} = 9\ \mathrm{nm}$, in the extreme ultraviolet.

**(c)** It is cooler by a factor of about 40. The luminosity grows in proportion
to the mass, but the radiating area grows as the *square* of the mass, because
$R \propto r_S \propto M$. So the luminosity per unit area — which is what sets
the temperature — goes down as the black hole gets heavier: at a fixed fraction
of Eddington, $T \propto M^{-1/4}$. The lower Eddington fraction and the larger
ISCO make it cooler still.
::::

## Summary

- **Lectures 1–2:** the Schwarzschild radius, $r_S = 2GM/c^2$, sets every black-hole length scale; spin
  moves the horizon and the ISCO inward and opens an ergosphere; tidal forces
  go as $M/d^3$, and at the horizon as $1/M^2$.
- **Lecture 3:** moving clocks run slow, moving lengths contract along the
  motion only, and light from an approaching source is blueshifted.
- **Lectures 4–5:** gravity is curved spacetime, tested by bending light,
  precessing orbits, and clocks and light that lose energy climbing out of a
  gravitational well.
- **Lectures 6–9:** falling matter turns a fraction $\eta$ of its rest mass into
  light; the Eddington limit caps the luminosity and so the growth rate; a
  higher efficiency means slower growth.
- **Lecture 10:** gravitational-wave strain falls as $1/d$, not $1/d^2$.
